#4028. The Sunday Papers

Sundays are for looking upon my DIY works and despairing. Strewn sawdust, spilled paint, and hunks of broken MDF litter my living room kingdom. When will it be over? When will I be free? When will I be able to reassemble my sofa, sit down with a cup of tea in hand, and admire my books, unpacked and arranged on perfectly fitted alcove bookshelves?

The Sunday Papers is our weekly roundup of great writing about (mostly) videogames from across the web.

"Today?" I whisper hopefully in response to a paragraph of rhetorical questions. "Probably not," snaps back Reality. Especially if I don't get out of bed soon. Still, here in bed I can read the best writing about and not about games from the past week.

Inside our Gchat walls, there is a growing exhaustion with genAI stories. Every day another gaming boss talks about the inexorable march of the tech before putting out a trailer filled with blurry text and six-fingered characters. I don't doubt the tech is getting better, but it's not inevitable. As such, Rob Fahey's latest GI column is something of a balm:

There is currently a concerted and not-so-subtle campaign underway to try to manufacture consent for the use of AI in game development.

At its core, this is about presenting AI as a fait accompli. Every week or so we get a new report making dubious claims about almost every development studio already using AI. The message to developers is "you'll be left behind if you don't use it too"; to players, it's "this is already done and there's no turning back". Consume like good little consumers. Shut up and eat your slop.

A further tonic comes from Merritt K, who writes for Aftermath about the technological improvements rolling through Karaoke.

Doesn't it feel like everything — especially everything Big Tech touches — is getting worse? Generative AI, not merely content with robbing humans of our craft and jobs, has escaped containment into physical reality in the form of shitty event flyers and small business signage. Hugely profitable industries like video games and film are being torn apart by the financialization of the economy as shareholders seek ever-increasing short-term profits. Algorithmic pricing of rent and groceries threatens to further punish the working class for the crime of not being born rich.

But in the heart of despair, we must reach for that which is good and pure and — dare I say it — better than it used to be. Karaoke is one of those things. And it is better not because of the disruption of tech giants, but, as is often the case, thanks to the work of enterprising maniacs toiling in obscurity, purely out of the love of the game.

I've been playing Forbidden Solitaire this week, where FMV sequences starring Xalavier Nelson Jr as an obsessive fantasy-author-turned-video-game-developer are played for laughs. So it was with a minor sense of whiplash I read Ashley Bardhan's piece for This Week In Video Games. Bardhan speaks to horror developers inserting themselves into FMV games to confront and explore violence against women.

Cara Cadaver uses her own photos and videos to represent multiple victims of sexual violence and murder in her unflinching 2025 game Vile: Exhumed. She tells me over email, “Being a woman is inherently a horrifying and violent experience, any way you slice it. One of my inspirations for making games in general is pulling from real-life experience and telling stories that most every woman has lived in some way; that’s real horror.”

“Horror in general has been a major outlet for me while dealing with trauma, and so much of horror as a genre goes back to women,” Cadaver says. “Women’s stories belong in horror — and that has been the case as long as horror has existed.”

Over at RPS-but-it's-The-Fade, Brendan's run through what made Bioware games great (and also terrible).

Bioware established romance as a must for any blockbuster RPG worth its frost salts (and not just RPGs).

Kissing your friends on the mouth is everywhere in mainstream and indie games today. It's a verb now. Characters are "romanceable". I played Nivalis Nights last month and could not get away from the swarms of horny NPC citizens trying to jump my noodle serving bones. Baldur's Gate 3 launched with a bug that made your companions fuckable in just a few nights, and people didn't even notice. They thought: that's normal and right, I should shag everyone, gender and orientation be damned. See that mountain? You can fuck it. And that's (at least partially) thanks to Bioware.

GTA is an unignorable thing. It is one of those breakout cultural objects that has its own gravity, drawing in attention and comment from politicians, mainstream press, parents, schools, comedians, columnists, footballers, taxi drivers, and hairdressers. In all the weight of it, I hadn't yet really seen it as a game. Simon Parkin's Edge cover feature may not reveal many new details about the game but it has made me appreciate it as a game (and maybe even get a little bit excited for its eventual PC release.

Nelson, grave-faced but friendly, wearing all black, with grey-flecked stubble, settles into a leather-and-chrome Eames chair while we perch on a burnt-orange sofa facing a pair of expansive wall-mounted TVs. In the past, Rockstar has carefully stage-managed encounters such as this. For previews of previous GTAs, one team member played the game while a publicist read from a pre-prepared script, further evidence of the paranoia that can take hold when an artist is working on something the entire world is desperate to see.

Today, however, Nelson has no script and, apparently, no plan. For the next 90 minutes he simply plays the current build, following his nose, confident that the game's systems will hold together wherever he pushes them, that this world's glories will glint and shimmer no matter which angle he approaches from. It is an extraordinary demonstration not of paranoia but of trust – in the game, in the team that built it, perhaps even in us.

Nelson picks up the controller and lets Grand Theft Auto VI speak for itself.

I am guilty of forgetting and looking away, but the humanitarian crisis in Gaza has not ended, it is deepening. Writing for the LRB, Selma Dabbagh bluntly captures the ugly events of the past two years :

In January 2025 Donald Trump described Gaza as a ‘demolition site’. ‘You’re talking about probably a million and a half people,’ he said, ‘and we just clean out that whole thing.’ The number is closer to two million people – not a ‘whole thing’ but two million individual human beings – who have been driven into an area that’s less than a third of the densely inhabited land they lived on. Their cities and arable lands – palms, olives, coriander, citrus and pomegranate trees – have been obliterated.

I'd like there to be a big reason for this week's music recommendation, but really it's just a little victory lap. I managed to nab some tickets to see This Is The Kit, so give Bashed Out a listen, yeah?

#4027. Dataminer uncovers that Spiny - a character seemingly with no way to operate a car - was meant to be playable in Mario Kart World

A dataminer has uncovered something peculiar in the code of Mario Kart World. Spiny, a tiny little turtle-looking fella with a spiky shell, was meant to be a driver in the game.

This information was discovered by Bluesky user Benial, with Spiny's internal name 'Togezo' listed alongside a selection of other characters. As of writing there's been no model, animation, nor idea of how exactly Spiny would imagine such a feat discovered.

Spiny, for those who don't know, is a menacing creature not particularly known for its driving prowess. 'Spiny' has long been the name for the enemies initially introduced in Super Mario Bros., and has been a staple of the Mario universe since 1985. With that angry look on his face and the spikes lining his shell, one would worry whether it's a good idea to let them behind the wheel at all.

Hey, why not? Boo is a playable driver, and the veteran ghost character also doesn't seem like the driving type. So Spiny may have made a great addition to the roster. Why is it my business whether Spiny has trouble driving a car or not; No one elected me to police the Rainbow Roads.

Mario Kart World is a great racing game that seems to have done well, even without Spiny behind the wheel. The game, as a Nintendo Switch 2 launch title, was present during the console's strong sales last year. The game has since received a selection of updates since its release, including a battle mode and team races to its tour mode.

#4026. It looks like footage of a Persona 1 remake has leaked, and if it's legit I really hope you don't hate the colour purple

I'm sure the artist formerly known as Prince would have loved it, at least

In this genAI world, every single leak that makes its way out into the world should be seen as more of a "leak" until proven otherwise. With that said, it does kind of seem like a remake of the first Persona game is on the way, with some footage supposedly leaking and showing it in action.

The leaked footage was shared yesterday to the GamingLeaksAndRumours subreddit, originally uploaded to the file-sharing site Gofile on Halloween, i.e. yesterday, i.e. October 31st. You will not at all be surprised to hear that, stylistically, it's incredibly in line with the vibe of contemporary Persona, a la the visual design established with Persona 5 that's been carried through to the Persona 3 and 4 remakes.

There's not a whole lot of footage to actually look at, just shy of two minutes all told. One bit shows the game's protagonist walking through a school at night before starting a battle. Again, the battle system looks like what you'd expect from Persona, being turn based and whatnot. The colour theme for this one is overwhelmingly purple, too, which at least lines up with the series' 25th anniversary artwork. What's perhaps slightly odd is that Persona 2's protagonist can be seen in battle; not sure if this is implying a combination of the two games, if two remakes are being made in tandem and it's a temporary use of assets, or if it's just an odd placeholder.

Persona 1 and 2 remakes wouldn't exactly be much of a surprise. Ashley interviewed series producer Kazuhisa Wada not too long ago, and he literally said "Persona 1 and 2 are something we’ll probably eventually do too." A knowing tease from Wada, perhaps? Who knows! Either way, the gameplay on display here looks believable, and Sega's leakier than a broken faucet (various Persona bits have leaked in the past too), so, something to keep an eye on at the very least, even if best taken with a pinch of salt.

#4025. Celeste and TowerFall dev explains why both games were suddenly delisted from Xbox

"We did this to support the BDS boycott."

Celeste and TowerFall have both been delisted from Xbox suddenly earlier this week. Per a post on Bluesky, developer Maddy Thorson says this was an intentional move, with the games being removed from sale on Xbox in support of the BDS (Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions) movement, which is aimed at protesting various companies linked to, or supporting, Israel's government during the genocide in Palestine.

"For those who're asking, yes we delisted Celeste and TowerFall on Xbox," states Thorson in a BlueSky post. "We did this to support the BDS boycott."

In case you're unaware, Xbox's inclusion on the BDS list is due to Microsoft's partnership with Israel and its prison system, according to BDS itself. The company has provided the country use of its Azure Cloud and AI systems, which have been used consistently over the past few years in the ongoing subjugation of Palestinians. BDS has urged people to cancel their Game Pass subscriptions, boycott leading Xbox franchises - including Call of Duty and Candy Crush - and cease purchases of Microsoft gaming products. As it stands, Celeste and TowerFall are now completely unavailable for purchase within the Xbox ecosystem.

This isn't the first time we've seen developers intentionally opt out of sales on Xbox because of the BDS movement; just a few weeks ago, Big Walk developer House House released a statement noting that its game is not on Xbox because of Microsoft's ties to Israel, and we saw the developer of Tenderfoot Tactics do the same in 2025.

"We would love for people to be able to play the game on Xbox, but not until Microsoft and/or Xbox have been removed as BDS boycott targets," noted the Australian developer at the time. "We've made this decision with the belief that meaningful change can be made in the world, that coordinated collective action can confront even the most powerful interests, and that one day, Palestine will be free."

Microsoft has responded to the BDS boycott previously, acknowledging that it supplied AI technology to Israel's Ministry of Defense, but claims "no evidence" it's been used to "target or harm people in the conflict in Gaza". Various reports, including the one linked above, refute this claim.

Celeste and TowerFall both remain available for purchase on PlayStation, PC, and Switch.

The world of game localization has lost a legend. Neil Broadley, the localization director on the SaGa series, recently passed away, and tributes from the series' community have been pouring in for him.

His death was announced through his own Twitter account, where a post prepared by Broadley appeared on November 6, published by one of his colleagues. In it, he explains that he'd been suffering for some years with stage four colon cancer, and is now survived by his long-time partner and their dog.

He actually worked through the discomfort of the ongoing treatments he'd undertaken in that time, continuing to translate various releases for Square Enix. "My work had been very healing for through-out the entire ordeal," he writes.

"Continuing on made me feel like my life had purpose," he adds. "I unfortunately will not be around to see the release of my next project, but I am extremely confident that you will enjoy it."

He reveals he was able to bring in his successor, who'll take on the mantle of localizing the SaGa franchise and making sure the long-running fantasy games continue to grow and prosper among English-speaking players. Broadley leaves big shows in that endeavor, because SaGa's enjoyed rejuvenated attention the last while, and his efforts in localizing the games have been crucial to that.

Comments of rest in peace are being left on an interview he did with Square Enix last year, for the release of SaGa Emerald Beyond. His post and a repost from the franchise's official account have replies turned off, but going by the sentiment over there, you can imagine what people are thinking.

"We are deeply saddened by the passing of Neil Broadley, who served as localization director for the SaGa franchise," reads a post on the series account. "On behalf of everyone involved with the franchise, we extend our heartfelt condolences to his family and loved ones."

#4021. What remains of canned Portal prequel white whale F-Stop is now fully playable thanks to modders and some big leaks

If you're something of a Portal or Half-Life head, you'll probably already be familiar with F-Stop, an unreleased Portal prequel that remained quite mysterious for many years. Back in 2020, a much deeper look was revealed in a semi-official capacity, revealing a pretty neat concept (that isn't so dissimilar to that of Superliminal). Now, all these years later, assets and source code for the game has leaked, and what exists of F-Stop is fully playable.

As spotted by Kotaku, the Valve Cut Content team and a number of leakers have been able to put together a playable version of F-Stop so that you can try it out for yourself. Mechanically, it works like so: you take a picture of an object, and said object disappears, turning it into a photo. You can then use this photo to rematerialise the object, sometimes changing the scale of it to help you navigate particular puzzles. It's cool! Just not something Valve thought was worth going all in on, evidently.

So the story goes, Valve overlord Gabe Newell did actually quite like the early version of the game that never was, it's just it didn't test all that well. I do kind of think that this is a lesson in not always listening to test audiences; the aforementioned Superliminal really is quite similar in execution, even tonally it's on the same kind of wavelength, and it ended up being quite a tight little experience that ended up being received quite positively, generally. In the end, bits of F-Stop were Frankensteined into Portal 2, so, at least we got that out of it!

The reason for the delay in being able to play F-Stop in this unofficial capacity is because of the crucial source code and map data. Back in August about 12TB of Steam data leaked, but that only contained the assets for F-Stop. Mods in the Valve Cut Content Discord server said that the person who leaked the F-Stop mapsrc asked for $1000 before just handing over the data in any case. Glad they did, $1000 bucks is a lot, I wouldn't pay it myself. Cool little bit of history to be found here, shame it never materialised in the way it was meant to.

Finding the Phantom Blade Zero Training Grounds Key took me ages, all because I missed a dirt path in the main Mandate camp that leads to the dovecote and, eventually, the boss that holds the key. It's also a very good idea to find it as you won’t be able to finish repairing the Illusory Pipa without it – and you'll miss out on some other rewards too. Anyway, I've explained exactly how you find the Training Grounds Key in Phantom Blade Zero below, so that you can wrap up the Mandate Encampment region and crack on with the main quest.

The Training Grounds Key is a reward for defeating the Chief Disciple of the Seven-Stars Formation boss fight in the middle of the Mandate Encampment. However, the critical path you need to take to reach this boss can be easily missed:

With the Chief Disciple boss defeated, the Mandate Encampment's Training Grounds Key will be yours – and the Phantom Blade Zero Moji's House Key is also just ahead! Now you just need to make your way to the Training Grounds door and interact with it to get it open. I won't spoil what's on the other side besides another boss fight, which rewards you with the flashy dual-wield Baishan Stormswords and the Broken Vessel Accessory (it doesn't quite make it onto my list of the best Phantom Blade Zero Accessories, unfortunately).Crucially though, you'll also find the backplate of the Illusory Pipa, which puts you one step closer to being able to take this mystical musical instrument to Myst in Pangzhen for repairs. And there are plenty of other collectibles to hoover up in this area, including the Lament Draught Medicine.Make sure you've also found the Phantom Blade Zero Village of Lu Cellar Key and Phantom Blade Zero Cell Key back in Weeping Creek Valley.

"I'm worried about everything all the time, despite being very laid-back. We've seen more of Grand Theft Auto 6 than we were meant to at this stage. All we were meant to have was a Netflix special, some sparse previews, and a very late launch trailer. But thanks to a certain leaker, some players have been able to see way more than we ever imagined.

This was both good for those who wanted to see more of the game before forking over $100 for its ultimate edition, and bad for the players who wanted an unsullied first look at GTA 6. The leaks gradually escalated, with the party responsible even threatening to leak the entire build and declaring they'd activate a dead man's switch if Take-Two pursued legal action against them.

"Because of the file sizes and the complexity, piracy is less of an issue in interactive entertainment, but it's not been a non-issue," Zelnick says. "And in the event where it turns into an issue we address it in the same way every other business does, which is with legal work and then with technical work, and we'll have to do both." And it's done exactly that. Despite the threats, Take-Two subpoenaed Discord for more user information concerning the leaks, which has since been granted by a court.

"I think it's fair to say that piracy is going to be an issue in our business going forward—we're just going to have to be vigilant about it," Zelnick adds. "Now, it's a little more complex because for all of our games you have to be connected with our servers to have a good experience. So with piracy are you really going to set up competitive servers? Is it really going to be a good experience? It won't be a great experience. But it's not nothing."

#4018. Japanese Rural Life Adventure now available for PS4

Publisher G-MODE Corporation and developer GAME START LLC have released a PlayStation 4 version of slow life simulation game Japanese Rural Life Adventure via PlayStation Store for $19.99 / £15.49 / €18.99 / ¥2,750, the companies announced. PlayStation Plus users can purchase it at a 20 percent-off discount price of $15.99 / £12.39 / €15.19 / ¥2,200 until November 20.

Japanese Rural Life Adventure first launched for Apple Arcade on September 15, 2023, followed by Switch and PC via Steam on March 3, 2026.

Here is an overview of the game, via G-MODE Corporation:

A relaxing slow-life simulation game where you can experience the charm of traditional Japanese countryside living, all in a beautifully crafted pixel-art world.

Japanese Rural Life Adventure is a relaxing slow-life simulation where you can experience the charm of traditional Japanese countryside living, all in a beautifully crafted pixel-art world.

Live in the Japanese Countryside Surrounded by Nature

Fix up an old house, make the yard nice, grow your own crops, and become self-sufficient.

View the cherry blossoms in the spring; attend the festival in the summer; eat roasted sweet potatoes in the fall; hear the temple bell ring in winter, and then it’s time for the first shrine visit of the New Year.

Rice—the essential source of energy for the people in Japan. Salt, soy sauce, miso—seasonings no Japanese kitchen can do without. In this countryside, many things city dwellers take for granted must be made by hand.

By standing in the kitchen or cooking around the traditional irori hearth of your heritage home, you can simulate preparing a wide variety of dishes and seasonings. Food made through your own effort tastes extra special.

Don’t be surprised if the game makes you hungry!

Bring Back Life to the Village Through Various Events

Many events unfold depending on the season, location, and time of day. A villager might ask you to repair an old waterwheel, or to help reopen a shuttered candy shop.

Strengthen your relationships with the locals and restore the liveliness the village once had. As you complete requests and interact with the villagers, you may earn useful items or unlock new areas to explore.

Your journey begins as the protagonist, a newcomer from the city, starts a solitary life in an old countryside house.

Start by clearing the overgrown weeds, cleaning the floors, and repairing the “shoji” paper screens.

By the time you’ve completed the tutorial, you’ll have learned the basics of village life.

Each morning, an elderly woman visits to sell daily necessities, and each afternoon, a man arrives to buy items you no longer need. Buy and sell goods as you steadily gather everything required to thrive in the village and complete your missions.

#4017. Dune: Awakening's seasonally appropriate Blood and Ice expansion gets a December release date, and in a plus for preservation, an offline mode this month

December is certainly going to be the month of Dune. The biggest Dune of Dunecember will obviously go to Dune: Part 3, which is Duen out December 18th. A little bit before that, however, is a well-timed free expansion coming to Dune: Awakening. It's called Blood and Ice, which sounds gross, but hey, I guess free blood and ice isn't entirely a bad thing?

"The expansion introduces the Polar Sink, an entirely new survival map where everything you've learned about surviving in the desert will be put to the test," explains a Steam blog post. "Instead of protecting yourself from extreme heat, you'll need to find ways to stay warm. The technology you've developed to survive the desert won't be enough here, and you'll need to upgrade your equipment, gather new resources, and adapt your strategies to survive the cold."

You'll find two biomes in the Polar Sink, the tundra and the ice cap, the former being where you'll kick off your time in this expansion. "While conditions here are more manageable than on the ice cap itself, these families won't welcome anyone interfering with their operations," the blog notes. Your main goal is to get the ice cap and gather up all of its valuable resources, namely, ice! Said ice can then be used to "cool your base equipment and speed up production."

Apparently you'll get about 35 more hours of "new progression, along with new vehicle modules, augments, and specialization traits," out of the expansion, and there are plans for future updates that'll give you reason to come back to the Polar Sink in Duen time. Beyond that, there is also a new cosmetic store, which lets you purchase "optional cosmetic items, including outfits, vehicle variants, and additional ways to customize your bases." I'm sure this will go down well.

Perhaps most importantly, this November will see the arrival of offline mode, meaning you don't need an internet connection to play it. Hopefully if (probably when (sorry to be a pessimist (realist))) the servers go down, this means it'll still be playable. Character copying so that you can copy your character from multiplayer servers to single-player will be coming in January, alongside full cross-play. Lots coming essentially!

#4016. Bethesda reportedly revealing The Elder Scrolls 6 next month, and we may know what its subtitle is going to be

Bethesda's hugely anticipated and long-awaited fantasy role-playing game The Elder Scrolls 6 could be revealed "as soon as next month", a new report has claimed - right in the midst of Microsoft's ongoing restructuring efforts.

Per The Verge, this new Elder Scrolls adventure carries the subtitle "Sentinel", which aligns with fan speculation, and the outlet corroborated prior reports that the game takes place within the Tamriel region of Hammerfell. The game reportedly touches on "history of the Elder Scrolls" and will "help uncover the secrets of these mysterious ancient artifacts".

If the game is revealed next month - presumably The Game Awards in early December is a good place for it - it would mark eight years after The Elder Scrolls 6's initial reveal trailer, and 15 years since the release of The Elder Scrolls 5: Skyrim. So, it's certainly been a while, though it's worth noting that The Elder Scrolls: Online has operated all through this period, to give fantasy fans something to bide their time with.

Asha Sharma, CEO of Xbox, said she'd played the game in August on a trip to the Bethesda offices, all while a giant inflatable rat and a union protest took place outside. Indeed, this reveal would take place shortly after Bethesda suffered job cuts - as did many other Microsoft-owned studios - as part of Xbox's "reset".

Xbox has been keen to keep fans optimistic of its prospects during what is undoubtedly a challenging time for the business. Yesterday, Sharma said there was "more demand than consoles available" when addressing a 14 percent dip in Xbox hardware sales. Microsoft's latest 8-K filing - a mandated finance report publicly traded companies have to file to the SEC - states in plain terms that "Xbox hardware revenue decreased 29 percent driven by lower volume of consoles sold".

Sharma has also pointed to the record performances of Minecraft and World of Warcraft: Forever's open beta, and congratulated Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 for having its "most acclaimed release in more than a decade". But Xbox's first-party release Gears of War: E-Day reportedly only sold more than 400,000 copies across Xbox and PC, following its day-one Game Pass launch. Analysts speculate that its presence on the service potentially cut into its full-cost sales.

All the while, we're seeing studios decide to not sell their game on Xbox altogether due to the company's presence on the BDS boycott list. Earlier this month, Big Walk's developers declared the game would not come to Xbox because of Microsoft's ties with Israel. And last night, both Celeste and Towerfall were removed from Xbox for the same reason.

So it's safe to say that The Elder Scrolls 6, if it is revealed next month, will arrive into a very different world than the one it poked its head into almost a decade ago. Whether it can help Xbox turn things around: that's the question.

#4015. There are currently "no other Assassin's Creed remakes actively in development", says Ubisoft

Yesterday, Ubisoft issued a statement about the future of the Assassin's Creed series, and the publisher's comments included quite a big surprise: there are currently no new remakes of the series' past games in the works.

"One thing we want to be transparent about today is that we currently have no other Assassin’s Creed remake actively in development," Ubisoft said in a statement on its website. "Our teams are already focused on the next chapter of Assassin's Creed titles, including projects you haven't heard about yet, featuring new settings and stories."

This has come as a shock to some players because, back in 2024, Ubisoft CEO Yves Guillemot specifically mentioned that upcoming remakes - plural - were in active development across Ubisoft studios. "Firstly, players can be excited about some remakes, which will allow us to revisit some of the games we've created in the past and modernise them; there are worlds in some of our older Assassin's Creed games that are still extremely rich," Guillemot said.

Given the success of this year's Black Flag Resynced - which sold over 3.5 million copies and "exceeded annual expectations within its first 14 days" - it's interesting to hear Ubisoft move away from what clearly seemed a popular way of revisiting older games. But it's worth noting that although Ubisoft isn't currently working on remakes, that doesn't mean we won't get them at some point in the future.

"Like many of you, we love the idea of revisiting our classic titles, and we'll keep exploring opportunities to bring older titles back," the company's statement continued. "That door remains open because, after all... Nothing is true, everything is permitted." That last bit, if you're unfamiliar, is a commonly-repeated motto amongst the Assassin Order.

If you're curious about what's next for the franchise, we've got a few ideas. First, there's 'Codename Invictus', which is billed as a "PvP multiplayer Assassin's Creed experience" being led by a team of For Honor veterans at Ubisoft Montreal. The title remains shrouded in mystery, and we've seen nothing of how the game will look or play yet.

Then there's Assassin's Creed Hexe, in development at Ubisoft Montreal. This game is touted as a "darker, narrative-driven" experience that appeared to be aiming for a 16th century European setting when it was announced back in 2022. It was originally believed to be targeting a 2026 release, but earlier this year, Ubisoft head of franchise Jean Guesdon explained the publisher is "taking the time to deliver on its ambitious vision, which means we'll be quiet for a little longer". Following this, a report emerged in August stating that Hexe is still at least a year away.

The Assassin's Creed series remains a pillar of Ubisoft's output, even if the publisher has been enduring a lot of change lately. Late last year, the leader of the Assassin's Creed franchise, Marc-Alexis Côté, left Ubisoft. This coincided with a reorganisation of the company and the creation of the Vantage Studios subsidiary, established by Ubisoft and Tencent, to oversee development of the French publisher's biggest franchises, which includes Assassin's Creed.

#4014. Gag Order is a co-op, SCP-ish horror shooter about surviving as best you can against some nasty, tentacle covered cephalopod creatures

Don't let it touch me, please and thank you

What makes Carrion interesting obviously lies in playing as the monster in a horror game rather than being the one chased down by it. The game's nasty tentacle monster still gives me the heebie jeebies, so I really would hate to be hunted by one. This is where I point you towards Gag Order, a shooter where you are in fact hunted by a disgusting cephalopod creature all while tracking down a distress signal.

Gag Order is not designed to be played solo, it feels wrong to call it friendslop given how unfriendly it is in vibes, but it does feel like it fits into a similar lineage as Lethal Company at the very least. In it, you are a research lab's Guardian Unit member, and you get a distress call "from one of the core parts of the complex." Upon arrival, the atmosphere is rotten, and you quickly come to understand that you are not equipped for what you have to deal with.

The solution, then, is to take care of those nightmare-inducing cephalopod creatures. Except during the first phase of a run, it sounds like they're invincible. Your guns do seem to be able to fend them off at the very least, but it's the second phase, which is geared around a "fast paced team-bossight" where it sounds like you'll be trying to take these things down. I'm not quite sure what the process is to get between those two phases, but I'm quite fond of the vibes on display.

It feels a touch reminiscent of 2000s shooters with some slightly contemporary mechanical sensibilities. I'm fond of the light SCP vibes it has going on, alongside the faint surrealness of certain elements like a bunch of crows hanging out in an abandoned office building. Creepy! Good looking stuff. Gag Order is apparently due out by the end of 2026, though we're obviously getting close there, so it's worth keeping an eye on it by throwing it a wishlist on Steam, if it takes your fancy.

#4013. Games industry honours beloved actor Sir Patrick Stewart, as the legendary Star Trek and X-Men actor passes away

"An emperor, a captain, and an inspiration to us all."

As I'm sure you're all now already aware, legendary British actor Sir Patrick Stewart has died, aged 86. His Instagram account announced the news yesterday, saying he died at home in Los Angeles surrounded by friends and family, following "a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia".

Stewart, a poised and charming actor, was probably best known for his on-screen roles as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation, and Charles Xavier-slash-Professor X in various X-Men films. But he also enjoyed a long and celebrated career on stage.

Stewart appeared in games, too, most notably in Bethesda's fourth Elder Scrolls game, Oblivion, as Emperor Uriel Septim 7th. He effectively kicked the adventure off, narrating the game's intro with gravitas before appearing as Septim to the player in their prison cell. There, he declared he'd seen the player in his dream and proceeded to let us free.

"I️ was born 87 years ago," Stewart's opening monologue began. "For 65 years I've ruled as Tamriel's emperor. But for all these years I've never been the ruler of my own dreams. I have seen the gates of Oblivion, beyond which no waking eye may see. Behold, in darkness a doom sweeps the land. This is the 27th of Last Seed, the year of Akatosh 433. These are the closing days of the Third Era, and the final hours of my life."

Bethesda, upon hearing of Stewart's passing, posted a picture of Emperor Uriel Septim from the recent Oblivion remaster, alongside the words: "Rest in peace to Sir Patrick Stewart - an emperor, a captain, and an inspiration to us all. Our thoughts are with his loved ones."

Stewart also notably voiced the narrator in both of MercurySteam's Castlevania: Lord of Shadows games, and appeared in a number of X-Men games and Star Trek games, as well as smaller projects like Polish Holocaust game My Memory of Us. In honour of his life and work, The Star Trek Online community gathered in large numbers, arranging spaceships in long lines to mark his passing.

Messages celebrating the person Stewart was have flooded social media overnight, written by the many people he impacted during his life and long career. Long-time X-Men collaborator and Wolverine actor Hugh Jackman said: "We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today. And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days."

And Sir Ian McKellen, the Magneto actor who was considered one of Stewart's best friends, gave an overview of the many years the two had known each other, from being "ambitious young actors with the Royal Shakespeare Company half a century ago", to working on X-Men together. McKellen recalled cautioning Stewart about taking the lead role in Star Trek because of the effect it would have on his stage career - advice Stewart fortuitously overrode. McKellen referred to his friend as "the most respected and beloved actor of his generation on either side of the Atlantic".

Rest in peace, Sir Patrick Stewart. There won't be another like you.

#4012. As if the injury descriptions weren't already ghastly enough in Dwarf Fortress, the legendary outpost builder is getting a "meat biome"

"Lots of meat terrain - muscle, bone, vertebral walls, sinew, sphincters."

Legendary outpost builder Dwarf Fortress is getting a meat biome. A terrible netherworld of bone and artery. A sunken redoubt of gristle and gizzard. An appalling labyrinth of squirt and squelch. Honestly, the biggest shock here is that Dwarf Fortress doesn't appear to have a meat biome already. It certainly has plenty of florid descriptions of fatal injuries.

These foul omens arrive care of a massive "Future of the Fortress" thread on the Bay 12 forums, in which studio co-founder (and prominent genAI disliker) Tarn "Toady One" Adams fields questions about the on-going development. As a forum thread, it's not a formal news source, so please season these tales of gutsy geology with whatever Condiment of Scepticism you consider appropriate.

There's no date for when the new biome might arrive, but Adams says it'll likely exist underground, and will be revolting. "Lots of meat terrain - muscle, bone, vertebral walls, sinew, sphincters," he promised. "We would have rivers of blood/fluids if we ever get to the fluid update, but no new fluids as it stands. We had thrown out the idea for maple syrup style taps on the vertebral walls for cosmic spinal fluid but alas, this is not in the game." At the very least, there won't be any meat trees, but you can mine the meat for resources.

Adams doesn't discuss the origins of the meat biome in the thread – is it more of a headless, fungal phenomenon, or is there some kind of huge mammalian cadaver down there? If it's the latter, one consolation is that the meat biome can't be resurrected. "Ha ha, I don't think regular meat can be animated currently?" Adams remarked in response to a question about biomes of squirming, zombified meat. "So probably not."

The bulk of the conversation around Dwarf Fortress at present concerns forthcoming changes to the magic system, together with how arcane knowledge is categorised, transmitted, preserved and lost throughout each procedurally generated world. There's a lot of speculative chat about that in the Future of the Fortress thread, too much to cleanly summarise. It's saying something about the density and stature of Dwarf Fortress that the addition of flesh caves feels like an afterthought.

Developer Bay 12's current plans for the game also include a crystal biome, which I would say is the nicer option, but then I remembered that this is Dwarf Fortress, the game in which you might end up getting besieged by the ghosts of the very children you callously sent to hunt down a wild elephant. There is absolutely going to be something in the crystal biome that gives you nightmares. Dazzling, prismatic nightmares.

#4010. Skyblivion modders reveal a former volunteer is "threatening to sue for damages upwards of €30,000" over work on the unofficial Oblivion remake project

"I just hope that we can get this resolved as soon as possible and get on with the planned release"

The team behind Oblivion remake mod Skyblivion are being threatened with legal action by a former volunteer on the project, according a video posted by current lead Kyle 'Rebelzize' Rebel. The situation looks like it'll need resolving before the mod, which was originally set to release last year, can finally make its way out of the Imperial City sewers.

"Recently, a former volunteer who contributed to Skyblivion’s development departed the project," the Skyblivion team outlined in a written statement and a YouTube video presented by Rebel. "We want to be completely transparent with the community about what has happened since their departure. After they left the project, we had several discussions regarding the continued use and maintenance of his work. The main disagreement centered on their objection to our decompilation of parts of their work — a necessary step our team took to maintain functionality and fix issues in systems already built into the project after access to the original source code repository was revoked."

"To protect ourselves from more stress and try and ensure a clean break, we decided to take the high road," Rebel explained in the video. "We have removed that work entirely. Thankfully due to some of our volunteers stepping up and simply learning new skill sets, as well as help from prominent Skyrim modders and permissions to use and integrate existing Skyrim mods, we've been able to implement replacements that we think fit Skyblivion's needs, in some cases even better than what we had before."

However, Rebel and co claim that despite them making it "clear multiple times to this former volunteer that we have removed their contributions", the ex-Skyblivion dev is "threatening to sue for damages upwards of €30,000". They claim that the ex-volunteer's legal threats "demand personal information of multiple volunteers [on Skyblivion] including full names and addresses". Rebel noted that the team see these demands as "something that we are simply not willing to share with someone that we don't even know" and feel are "just completely disproportionate for what's really going on".

The modders say they've consulted with legal counsel already and have a lawyer on standby if necessary. Though, since said lawyer's services will - the Skyblivion team claim - cost €2,500, they've put out a call for anyone with "a background in IP law or GDPR law" willing to offer them pro bono legal aid to get in touch via the mod's website.

"Please don't turn this into any kind of witch hunt, despite this very unfortunate situation," Rebel said in closing. "We don't wish ill on a former volunteer over all this and I just hope that we can get this resolved as soon as possible and get on with the planned release, which is really what we're working towards. You will hear more from us soon on the actual release."

This situation makes it two years running that Skyblivion's found itself engulfed in drama during the final months of what's supposed to be its release year. In 2025, former volunteer Dee Keyes had a public disagreement with the project's leads over whether releasing the mod that year was a reasonable or achievable goal. Skyblivion was subsequently delayed into 2026.

This past weekend, Keyes tweeted a response to the Skyblivion team's statement on the alleged legal threats. "I've had my issues with the project and left because of it, but I left knowing that my work would remain with [Skyblivion] (happily so) and didn't want to hurt the project's progress," he wrote. "I understand [the former volunteer] being upset, but I really don't see why they'd go so far as to demand their work ripped out."

Here's hoping the Skyblivion team and the ex-volunteer can resolve things without all the expense and effort that'd inevitably be necessary if the dispute ends up in court. Given there are now less than two months left of 2026, and Skyblivion's modders have this on their plates on top of any remaining work needed to finish their creation, I'd personally be very surprised if its release doesn't end up being pushed into next year.

#4009. Sony has snapped up the film rights for Mouthwashing

Sony has snatched up the movie rights for Mouthwashing, the hit independent horror video game released in 2024.

Deadline reports Sony has obtained the rights from developer Wrong Organ and publisher Critical Reflex, and also brought on Karyn Kusama to direct the adaptation, a director perhaps best known for her work on the acclaimed Yellowjackets television show.

Sony has also enlisted Matt Manfredi and Phil Hay to write for the project, as well as production company Crooked Highway (who you may know for the Ethan Hawke–lead series of movies, The Black Phone). There is no word on which actors will star in the adaptation as of yet, nor whether the story will follow that of the game's own narrative.

Mouthwashing was a critically acclaimed release, and sold more than 500,000 copies as of February 2025. That was on PC alone, with the game made available on consoles yesterday.

This adaptation would arguably follow the path paved by the Iron Lung movie, created by Mark Fischbach (better known by his online alias Markiplier) and his own production company Markiplier Studios. That, a film adaptation of an indie horror game, performed exceptionally well at the box office bringing in $21m globally shortly after its premiere.

A Mouthwashing movie is an interesting idea. The main question is whether or not it would follow the plot and narrative structure of the game faithfully, or whether changes would be made to better suit the big screen. A sillier - but awfully tantalising - question, is who you'd like to see casted in the movie? Who'd play Swansea… Who'd play Jimmy?!? Questions abound.

#4008. Forza director, who'd been with Turn 10 for 27 years leaves Microsoft, following studios merger with Playground Games

Dan Greenawalt, director, founder, and vice president at Turn 10 Games, has departed from the studio after spending 27 years as part of the company. This comes as Turn 10 is merged with Playground Games as part of Xbox's mass restructuring initiative that made headlines as it resulted in 3200 layoffs and four studio closures earlier this year.

In a report by The Verge, an internal memo written by Playground Games studio head Trevor Williams states: "Dan Greenawalt has decided that this is the right time for him to retire from Microsoft".

The memo continues: "It's hard to overstate Dan's impact over the past 27 years. From shipping Project Gotham Racing on the original Xbox in 2001 to leading the creation of Forza, founding Turn 10 Studios and appearing so many times on our E3 stage, usually making a dramatic entrance with a supercar in tow – and so much more – we owe tremendous thanks and gratitude to Dan. On behalf of both teams, I would like to thank Dan for his leadership, his support, and his partnership. I wish him well for whatever comes next.".

With Xbox's merger of Playground Games and Turn 10, the developers will be working in collaboration on the Forza and Fable franchises. The final track racer game that Playground Games developed prior to this merger was 2023's Forza Motorsport reboot, a wonderful racer that offered a sweet alternative to the more arcade Forza Horizon series. In Eurogamer's review, the game was described as: "A generous and lavish racer, with thrilling driving, that wants you for the long haul.".

#4007. Delve into "a deep underground facility full of secrets and horrors" in the latest Fallout 4 quest mod from the Commonwealth Story Expansion Project

A mysterious bunker with out of this world contents

After adding a whole new town to Fallout 4 last month, a group of modders have released another in their long string of extra quests for the RPG. This latest mission revolves around a dungeon delve in the Glowing Sea, where a mysterious bunker's just been unearthed.

"The harsh radioactive winds of the Glowing Sea have uncovered a deep underground facility full of secrets and horrors," the group behind the Commonwealth Story Expansion Project (CSEP) declared the description of this latest work, Under The Stars.

A fresh dungeon with a quest attached, the mod tasks you with donning your hazmat suit for a trip to a sunken bunker in the region of post-apocalyptic Boston with the least chill weather. Inside await voiced holotapes and puzzles offering clues as to what went down in this cosy corner of the Commonwealth, plus some new gear to make braving whatever lurks within worth it.

Spoilers: Judging by the screenshots, it looks like the place is an Area 51-esque hidey-hole for evidence of aliens and other cryptic oddities.

If you're unfamiliar, the CSEP lot are responsible for a bunch of popular Fallout 4 quest mods based around the likes of deadly cults, underground wars, post-apocalyptic detective work, and Brotherhood of Steel drama. While Under The Stars doesn't look have been as big an undertaking as those, that previous form points to it being an expertly-crafted addition that'll slot seamlessly into the game.

The modders have put Under The Stars together as part of a community-hosted modding jam called Fallout Flood, with this latest one based around the theme of being underground. Among the other works to have come out of it thus far are another Fallout 4 quest mod dubbed Stranded - The Oasis, a dungeon full of funky rats called the S'Laven, and a new robot enemy you can wear as a hat. It's also produced a New Vegas quest mod about exploring an abandoned NCR railway, so seems to have been very productive gathering of modding minds.

To give Under The Stars a go, your copy of Fallout 4 will need to have the Automatron and Vault-Tec Workshop DLCs.

#4004. Fewer genAI clones of "someone else's specific game" should flood the net going forwards, as Anthropic tell Claude to stop messing with some stuff other people own

It will still let people generate "original" games using the tech

Anthropic have told their genAI tool Claude to start ducking requests from users to recreate or clone existing games, following a flood of folks using the tech to generate six-fingered remakes. Instead of risking infringing on the intellectual property of series or titles that companies which aren't Anthropic own, Claude will instead restrict itself to only generating "original" games slopped together based on whatever data it's drawing on.

"We added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy," Anthropic staffer Addy Osmani wrote on not Twitter in response to a rando with a cat profile picture having spotted the change.

"Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working," Osmani continued. "We'll continue to iterate to ensure we're striking the right balance. In the meantime, if Claude turns down something that's yours, send it my way." Game Developer reached out to Anthropic for confirmation and were pointed to Osmani's post.

The change should make it harder to add to the horde of genAI-powered decomps, recomps, and ports which have hit the net recently. It's hardly a surprising one, given studios like Bethesda have seemingly had to take matters into their own lawyers' hands to get the likes of an AI-generated Fallout game taken offline, with games that've just been ripped wholesale or barely tweaked likely on even more perilous ground. That said, not every corp's responded to the DIY decompilation craze by immediately taking legal action.

There's a serious degree of irony to Anthropic slapping Claude and telling it stealing is bad. One of the ways the company develop and train their genAI models is by scraping publicly available data from the internet via a web crawler.

So, some nicking of stuff is bad, little bot people keep asking to regurgitate stuff into slop they can then try to pass off as something they've created. But not all nicking of stuff, lest our whole business be on rather shaky ground.

It's unlikely this move from Anthropic does much to convince actual developers of original games they're safe to put demos of their games out prior to release, without risking dickheads using genAI to clone said demo and potentially release a slop version in rapid fashion, but one can dream of that genie being put back in the bottle someday.

#4003. Fix up towering robots while battle rages outside in Bay 12: Mech Repair, a first-person job sim with some handsome heavy duty analog tech

The most important thing to know about Bay 12: Mech Repair is that these are mechs of the MechWarrior or possibly Patlabor school – that is, basically WW2 tanks on hydraulic legs, with cockpits full of switches and wireframe displays. Their bodies are assemblages of pistons and reactors. They are not biomechs like the ones in Evangelion. An Evangelion Repair game would be… different. Less industrial, more Oedipal. You would dread removing the smallest piece of housing.

Which isn't to say that Bay 12: Mech Repair represents life on Easy Street, exactly. There's a big war happening outside, its fortunes palpable in the minced leg joints and pocked torsos of the war-bots lowered into your hangar. You're also fed details about the lives of pilots when you accept a work order. Lieutenant Iona Vale of the 3rd Recon Company says there's "left leg hesitation after extended operation", especially at higher temperatures. That sure sounds like a thing that could get Lieutenant Iona Vale killed.

It's not clear whether you can diagnose faults incorrectly, and shape the progress of the conflict, but the context brings extra emotional charge to what might otherwise be a cosy process of glueing together very expensive Air-Fix models, for all the sense of scale.

Bay 12: Mech Repair follows a familiar flow, as job sims go. Banged-up Iron Giants arrive in a steady procession. You figure out what's wrong with them based on scans, pilot reports, and so forth. Then you get out there with a welder, drill and spanner to make it right. Busted parts can be salvaged for scrap for custom components. Completed work orders net you credits that must be divided between restocking your inventory and buying new tools.

You also have the option of clearing away rust and applying a new paintjob. I'm fascinated to know if this has any real impact on either the story or your fortunes, because I guarantee that I am going to spend far more time obsessing over dazzle camouflage than giving the ol' actuators a haircut.

Read more on Steam. The devs, Crimson Herring Studios, are them wot did Sovereign Syndicate, an apparently decent Victorian fantasy RPG that we never found time to review. Look, I am not made of thumbs and eyeballs. As for the daunting possibility of an Evangelion Fixing Sim, the recently announced Valkyrie Iteration gets into some of the squirming detail, there.

#4002. You can make a vampire hunter who's afraid of the dark, disease and small spaces in Hunter: The Reckoning - Deathwish, and that's surely the best way to play

A month or two back I penned a 1500 word whine about feeling too powerful in Blood of Dawnwalker. "Gimme a vampire sim in which I'm a pathetic vein-nibbling goblin," I wrote, using many more adjectives than that. Well, never let it be said that I'm biased against vampires, for I am equally keen to play an RPG in which I am the least capable vampire hunter in the universe. A vampire hunter who screams when he wakes up with his hair over his face. A vampire hunter who has to spray the vampires with antibac before staking them.

An RPG like Hunter: The Reckoning – Deathwish, perhaps, which presents you with a choice of Advantages and Flaws when creating a character. You have to balance these out on a gnarly weighing scale, before they'll let you through the game's front door. Here is a video showing all that off, together with a lot of sixpacks.

The Advantage/Flaw system looks familiar on the surface. Advantages include Warrior, which gives you +15% chance of a critical hit, or Charmer, which gives you a +1 to Persuasion skill checks. Flaws include clumsy, bad reputation, fear of darkness, hypochondriac, and claustrophobia.

I don't know much about the tabletop game on which Deathwish is based, and the video skims the detail here, but I suspect the last three Flaws will boil down to something like "-1 Constitution in Unlit Closets". Still, I really enjoy the idiocy of going up against crypt-dwelling undead while being unable to tolerate shadows, small spaces, and disease. In general, I'd love it if Hunter: The Reckoning – Deathwish steered well away from any possibility of simply overpowering the vamps, to say nothing of the werewolves and other creatures of the night.

This appears to be the idea: devs Teyon have stressed their desire to make something more story and investigation-driven, after the stomping gibfest that was RoboCop: Rogue City. As narrative designer Mateusz Działowski put it in a previous dev diary, they've "switched from action with RPG elements into RPG with action elements". Amongst other things, you'll need to put together a team of fellow would-be slayers, each with secrets and traumas, and gather clues about best tactics while roaming the game's condensed and shiny New York City. You can read more about it all on Steam.

#4000. itch.io will soon let you filter games with genAI disclosures out of your search results on the site, after admitting it was previously "critically lacking"

itch.io has unfortunately, much like Steam, long had an issue with genAI content being uploaded in droves, drowning out perfectly good games made by human hands. The apparent standard method against this, voluntary genAI disclosure, has been itch's primary tool to combat this wave of low-quality slop, but hasn't worked out too well; itch revealed a few days ago that 'the number of game pages being created per-day has doubled in the past two months'. Now, in attempts to further combat this, beyond just game assets requiring a genAI disclosure to upload as they have for two years, itch will be expanding the mandatory disclosure to tabletop games, books, comics, and soundtracks, as well as adding a 'no AI' filter directly into the search function.

itch noted in this announcement that its previous moderation of genAI use in projects had been "critically lacking", presumably referring to the unfathomable exponential increase in games being uploaded in the past few months by people who don't give a fuck about creating anything themselves and happily contribute to the death of the planet. itch went on to post "Just deleted a couple terabytes of ai slop" which, I mean, sure, cool! And, look, as many, many people in itch's replies have pointed out, this is not the same as outright banning AI.

Unfortunately, my question at that point becomes: how? itch is not Steam, not a storefront backed by a gigantic corporation with support staff and quality assurance (which, you know, hasn't helped Steam much either). itch is one full-time employee with several contractors and volunteers. If there is a site-wide ban on genAI, people who use genAI will just start lying and sneaking it into their projects anyway. So, then, users just report the offenders, surely? This then requires a manual verification system, which, as is suggested by the sheer amount of games being uploaded every day, is just not feasible, let alone for a team as small as itch. And, frankly, I don't have a better solution here! This is fucked! What itch is doing is, currently, kinda the best it can right now?

itch is a beautiful thing that allows for people who just want to start making games, making art, making music, making books, to have a free space to share it with the world, and gain eyes on their work as well as necessary feedback to improve. It's less of a store and more of a forum for creators and self-published games to interact, guide one another to new, niche, cool shit. Hell, I made a visual novel and posted it on there, becoming another one of those millions of people for whom itch is a valuable platform for first creations. To have this vital space on a path to ruin as a result of the same vile tech that is also on the verge of pushing the global economy over a cliff due to its creators being caught in their multi-year lies is not a future I hope for itch. This is a step in the right direction, and one I genuinely hope pans out well for it in the long run.

I don't remember the last time I actually took a duster to my own rig. But in my defence, I only recently upgraded my motherboard and that required I remove pretty much everything out of my PC in the process of ripping out an old ASRock mobo I could no longer trust in favour of an Asus. So, that basic action meant that I had cleaned my PC by proxy in the past couple of months, though without actively cleaning it.

Which has me straddling both camps of PC Gamer reader, it seems. Because, while the biggest single majority of readers we polled can't remember when they last cleaned their PC, either, a healthy 45% of readers have actually given their rig a thorough once-over in just the past six months.

Now, I get that you have to change your bedding/towels/pants more often than that, but six months is but a mayfly's daydream in the life of your gaming PC. So, I applaud all of you taking rig maintenance so seriously.

This all came off the back of a recent weekly poll where we asked the question: When did you last dust/clean your gaming PC? Sure, over a quarter of you are living in filth, but I'm still proud of the rest of you.

When did you last dust/clean your gaming PC?

Along with the 26% who can't remember, there are another 14% of readers who haven't lifted a finger to dust their PC in over a year. Then there are the paragons of virtue, the children of the light, the 5% who cleaned their PC only that very day they saw the poll. Blessed ones.

But if you look at the numbers in total, we are a culture in balance. There's a healthy 45% of readers who have cleaned their machines in the past six months, and on the other side another 40% of readers who haven't touched their PC with a duster in over a year, with a 15% fulcrum in the middle who have spent time cleansing their rig in the past 12 months.

Equilibrium is everything, but where do you sit on the cleanliness teeter-totter? And how important is it to you?

#3998. EA reportedly closed BioWare because it was forced to choose between Mass Effect 5 and Star Wars Battlefront 3

And it chose the "less risky, more predictable bet".

A new report has revealed that EA closed BioWare because it was forced to choose between investing in one of two sci-fi projects: a new Mass Effect game or a new Star Wars Battlefront game. And it chose the latter.

The revelation comes from Bloomberg, which heard from "people familiar with the company's strategy" that the "recent emergence" of an opportunity to develop a third Battlefront game meant EA - a company saddled with $18bn in debt because of the recent leveraged buyout - would have two sci-fi projects, each likely to cost hundreds of millions of dollars to make.

It couldn't afford to make both of them so EA executives chose Star Wars Battlefront 3, because it was seen "as a less risky, more predictable bet than a new Mass Effect", Bloomberg reported - despite development for the game not even having begun yet.

An EA spokesperson said the company had "collectively reached this decision following months of planning, review, and analysis, including careful consideration of evolving business conditions, industry dynamics, and our long-term priorities". "While this is never easy," the spokesperson went on, "we ultimately have to make tough decisions to focus our teams on the biggest opportunities for our future, including investing in new projects across our portfolio."

The report highlights a few other contributing factors in EA's decision, including BioWare's unfavourable recent track record and a reorganisation of its executive ranks to include more EA Sports people, in favour of those advocating for BioWare. EA bosses even lamented Dragon Age: Veilguard's sales, suggesting it would have been better if the title was 'a live service game'.

Last week, following the announcement of BioWare's closure and the cancellation of Mass Effect 5, an internal video for the project - known as Mass Effect Universe - was leaked, showing what appears to be a pre-rendered visualisation of it. The game was said to take place 600 years after the Reaper war, in the midst of a galactic cold war, and to have the player be "a cross between John Wick and James Bond" in terms of what they'd be capable of.

There was a promise of "Hitman-style freedom" in approaching levels, romance that "wasn't being sanitised", and for connections between the Milky Way and Andromeda galaxies. It's not clear how much work was done on it, but clearly a lot of planning had been done - far more, certainly, than has been done on Battlefront 3.

EA's Star Wars Battlefront 2 was released in 2017 and struggled, initially, to convince - partly because it was riddled with loot boxes. But years of adjustments and improvements left it in a much better place.

The developer has hinted at multiplayer-focused DLC in the future, as well as a sequel to the popular game. If you're curious what took the world by storm earlier this year, you can try the free trial on your console of choice right now.

Of course, this isn't the first time the Dark Souls trilogy has had to contend with server problems. In 2022, Bandai Namco took servers for all three Dark Souls games offline due to a security vulnerability affecting Dark Souls 3. The threequel went dark once again a few months later.

FromSoftware's next game The Duskbloods - the one with the jetpacks and vampires and a cute bird thing - hasn't been any luckier, either. The multiplayer-focused game's first network test had to be taken offline early due to similarly vague "server issues". More recently, FromSoftware delayed its Switch 2 exclusive into next year.

"While development of The Duskbloods is at the final adjustment stage, we have made the decision to move the launch window to 2027," the developer tweeted this week. "We apologise to players who have been kindly awaiting the release of this title and thank you for your patience and support."

#3994. Blizzard hints at console ports for World of Warcraft: Forever - "Play it wherever you want and, at some point, on whatever you want"

After more than two decades dominating the PC MMO battlefield, it sounds like Blizzard Entertainment's taking the idea of a World of Warcraft console port more seriously than ever.

World of Warcraft: Forever's beta seems to have been immensely popular with fans of the series. It's a brand new third version of the iconic multiplayer game that sits alongside WoW's Classic and Retail portions, and it's recaptured many a lapsed Warcraft sicko with tons of good changes, big and small - one of which is controller support for the first time ever.

Speaking to GamesRadar about the decision to keep World of Warcraft: Forever exclusive to PC players, despite now supporting gamepads, vice president and executive producer Holly Longdale hinted that the fantasy game might just make its way to even more devices and players over time.

"What you just described is really what we're after," she told the outlet. "Play it wherever you want and, at some point, on whatever you want. But the first leg of that journey is getting gamepads working really well with World of Warcraft, and we thought Forever was the perfect place to start."

Longdale reckons all gaming platforms might become "more ubiquitous" in the future, as well. She specifically named the Xbox Project Helix, which is said to be a PC-console hybrid device of some kind. Xbox CEO Asha Sharma confirmed the next-gen console can even play your PC games earlier in the year.

"Honestly, we just want to be able to play it anywhere. We've seen people getting it working on the ROG Ally X," Longdale added. "I think just doing some of the work we're doing on gamepad is going to give players a lot of flexibility that I think goes beyond consoles."

World of Warcraft: Forever properly launches on the 4th of November.

Despite struggles in the rest of the Xbox division, Forever's beta was supposedly the "largest" in series history. Elsewhere, Longdale acknowledged that some of the developer's decisions won't make everybody equally happy: "I think the lesson we learned the most over time is 'You don't listen to the loudest people in the room.'"

For the foreseeable future, the devs aren't ready to talk about the kinds of DLC and spin-offs and follow-ups that dear old Shovel Knight enjoyed for many years, but they're not abandoning their newest baby either. Co-founder Nick Wozniac went further into the state of the developer, and why splitting the team in half was probably a mistake. Here's what he had to say on the matter: "Sales are the things that keep the company afloat so it's not born from greed (mostly) that we say we'd love to see more sales, it's all about continuing to work together and make great games and reaping the rewards along the way. #3992. A former volunteer is threatening legal action against fan-made game project Skyblivion

A former volunteer is threatening legal action against Skyblivion, the long-running fan remake of Oblivion built in Skyrim's engine, over code they contributed to the project.

The unofficial project, which remakes 2006's The Elder Scrolls 4: Oblivion, is being made by volunteers from the TES Renewal Project, the modding group that also works on Morrowind remake Skywind.

Bethesda has allowed the project to continue on condition that it replaces all of the original game's assets, and the team continued working on it after Bethesda released its own Oblivion Remastered in April 2025.

In a statement posted to Twitter/X on 30th October, the Skyblivion team said that after the volunteer left, the two sides disagreed over the "continued use and maintenance" of their work.

A former volunteer is attempting to sue Skyblivion and we need your help pic.twitter.com/3Ee5eQTELG

The main issue was the team's decompilation of parts of that code, which it said was needed "to maintain functionality and fix issues" after its access to the original source code repository was revoked.

According to the team, the volunteer then "escalated to sending legal threats", including demands for the real names and home addresses of its volunteer team leads. The team said this was "something we couldn't accept and think is disproportionate".

The team said it has consulted legal counsel and is "completely confident in our right to maintain the code they submitted". Even so, it said it removed the code "to protect our volunteers from undue stress and ensure a clean break", rebuilding that system from scratch.

Despite this, it says the threats have continued. Its post says the former volunteer is "attempting to sue", but it's not clear whether a lawsuit has actually been filed. The volunteer has not been named.

"Please don't make this a witch-hunt," the team told fans, adding that it wishes the former volunteer "the very best" and hopes to "get this resolved as soon as possible and get on with our planned release of Skyblivion".

Last December, the team delayed Skyblivion from 2025 into 2026.

#3991. "There’s always a night when Rome burns": South Of Midnight director says that Xbox funding it was "unsustainable", at least in hindsight

"I didn’t know exactly when it would be, but I was always worried about it"

Compulsion Games parted ways with former owners Xbox, having landed on the long list of things Microsoft were determined to ditch as part of multi-round mass cuts this year. Now, South of Midnight creative director David Sears has suggested that an eventual pulling of the rug was something he feared throughout the game's development, to the point where he seemingly doesn't think he'd have funded it if he'd been in the shoes of Xbox execs.

In an interview with MinnMax, Sears - who left Compulsion in March 2025 - outlined that ideally games big publishers put out aim to fall into one of two buckets. They either make lots of money or increase the prestige of the brand by becoming cultural touchstones across multiple generations. Obviously doing both is the perfect outcome, but Sears pegged South of Midnight as being more geared towards the latter camp. The likes of Double Fine's Keeper and Obsidian's Pentiment are other games which off the top of my head could be said to fit that same mold. The issue, of course, is that when push comes to shove, it's the games which can show a strong bottom line at any given moment which make the best case for their studios' short term survival if cash is tight.

So, South of Midnight lived in a risky place, with Sears recalling: "I literally told people. I was like, yeah, this could be terrible because somebody is going to say, one day, 'The money tap, we're closing those floodgates' and that's going to have really traumatic results downstream". The interviewer then asked Sears if what he was getting at is that, while he's glad Xbox funded South of Midnight, he might not have done so or at least cut the funding earlier if he was in charge of the console maker.

"Yeah, probably," Sears replied. "I mean, I wanted to make it. No doubt. Obviously, because we made it. Would I have turned off someone else's money flow before South of Midnight? Yeah, because I'm not completely selfless. It just seems like, in hindsight at least, it was unsustainable. So, of course, it was going to have a 'shocking' outcome. I mean, it's easy to dissect it now, right? But at the time, I would talk to other directors and [they] would be like, 'How is this happening? I mean, how did we get so lucky? Is this a golden era?' And I would always be like, 'For now'. There's always a night when Rome burns and I didn't know exactly when it would be, but I was always worried about it."

Notably, Sears added that in his view modern Microsoft showed a "more humane" side than the version of the company that existed in the 90s and early 2000s by giving studios like Compulsion a chance to spin out on their own rather than simply shuttering them outright once they were deemed surplus to requirements.

Given the director's no longer at Compulsion, it seems he'll not have a say on what their next game looks like, but as a newly indie studio one would imagine they'll have a keen eye on the bottom line.

#3989. Arc Raiders devs Embark insist that using genAI for voice lines was necessary, as "actors would just go crazy if they had to read all of that"

Despite taking the voice performances of actors and feeding them into machines to spurt out AI-generated mimicry, Embark CCO Stefan Strandberg insists that "we are not in the industry of replacing actors." In a new video posted to the Arc Raiders channel focused on audio design, Strandberg refers back to the infamous use of genAI in Arc Raiders to generate voice lines based on real voice actors' performances, something which the game was heavily (and rightly) criticised for before and since its release.

In that linked piece (thanks Oisin!), CEO Patrick Söderlund stated that they have been replacing lines that were originally generated with actual recorded lines, presumably because Arc Raiders has made quite a bit of money and now they feel that they can continue paying actors to record more lines, rather than just scraping their talents and avoiding the dreaded fee of paying professionals for their work. This choice already came after their previous game, The Finals, was heavily criticised for the exact same thing, which is just a fascinating series of decisions to consider.

In the video, audio director Bence Pajor explains that the apparent reason for the use of AI was to avoid the "stress" of having to work around actors' availability, as they may be busy working on other projects when Embark decides that a new feature needs new voice lines recorded. Pings, quests, and in-level mission briefings were thus generated using training data based on existing actors' recordings, saving the need to actually get anyone back in a studio or pay them for their time. Citing the amount of variables that the ping system creates, Pajor claims it "becomes too impractical to record every possible version of something. The actors would just go crazy if they had to read all of that", which is a take that falls apart if you consider the simple fact that games of this scope (or bigger) have been managing to work around actors' availability for as long as genAI has not been an accessible technology, which has been almost all of the time that video games have existed. Isn't it crazy that games like Disco Elysium and Baldur's Gate 3 had so, so much recorded dialogue, all without genAI? Or fellow live service shooter Apex Legends, which has been adding and adjusting voice lines via updates for years? How could they possibly have managed it?

Voice actresses Jo Rideout and Diana Gardner, who play Shani and Celeste respectively, are also featured speaking on their characters' relationships as well as their experience working within this hybrid model of recording and generating voices. Gardner notes that "if they only need an hour of my time for a couple call-outs that are short, then I don't have to cancel other shoots or some other project that might also be interesting. So in that way, I feel quite good about it." She then explains that "the contract seemed fair…so it was a no-brainer in that sense. But I didn't know what to expect once I heard the voice come out. I was like, 'Can I take ownership for the performance?' This is hours of work that I've put in, but can I take ownership for the final product? No."

Strandberg goes on to elaborate on his comment on not replacing actors by saying that "We are not in the industry of replacing actors, actually, I think quite the opposite. We should celebrate the performance, and we should give them more space." While Embark's audio team are indeed working on replacing the generated lines with actual performances, that doesn't change the fact that the choice to use AI in the first place was one made simply to save money in not paying actors for their specific work and get the game out the door faster — effectively the 'we'll fix it in post' of games development. While I can respect Garner's awareness that it means she can prioritise other projects when necessary, there is that notable tinge of regret in not being able to take ownership for her hours of work. Fundamentally, Embark has demonstrated its willingness to cut talent to cut costs, seemingly happy to post PR videos implying they had no choice due to the game's scope, and that isn't something a company just goes back on once they realise how 'efficient' it can be.
